title: Moon Phase Calculator: Phase and Illumination

summary_sentence: For example, for 22 October 2026 the dashboard reads: waxing gibbous, about 86% illuminated, age about 11.1 days, full moon roughly three days ahead — one date, the whole lunar story.

use_cases.title: Checking a claim about a date

body.t: Full moon at the wedding? Crescent for the crossing? The dashboard answers with the numbers exposed, not just the name — close calls show their margins.

Age 11.1 days is 75% of the way from new to full; the illumination formula turns that geometry into about 86% lit; the name for 'past quarter, not yet full, still growing' is waxing gibbous. Three readings, one Moon, zero contradictions.

Feed it 3 March 2026 and it reports full at ~100% — the night of a total lunar eclipse. Feed it 12 August 2026 and it reports new — a total solar eclipse. When a dashboard's extremes match the eclipse calendar, the middle values earn their keep.

popular_table.note: All readings derive from the mean synodic cycle (29.53059 days) — consistent with each other by construction, and within hours of the real sky's events in most cycles.

faq: How accurate are the milestone dates?
Mean-model milestones land within several hours of the true instants in typical cycles — good for planning evenings, not for timing eclipse contacts. Almanacs and ephemerides own the last few hours.
Why do the name and the picture sometimes disagree?
Phase pictures are drawn for band centres; a Moon at a band edge wears its neighbour's face. The dashboard's age number is the tiebreaker — trust it over the icon.
Is the phase the same worldwide?
Essentially yes at any instant — the whole Earth shares one Moon geometry. The date line means the same Moon can carry two calendar dates at once, which is a calendar fact, not a lunar one.
Humped — more than half lit, less than full, from the Latin for a hump. Waxing gibbous grows toward full; waning gibbous shrinks from it. The ugly word is the precise one.
Can it show the Moon for a historical date?
Yes — the cycle counts backward as happily as forward. Precision fades slowly over centuries, so a medieval date's phase name is a good estimate, not a sworn statement.
Why is the full moon sometimes a day off my calendar?

Printed calendars mark the date of the full instant in one timezone; the mean model can sit hours away, and your evening may precede the instant. Any of the three can move the label by a day near the boundary.
Does it include moonrise and set?
This dashboard is phase-first. The Moonrise and Moonset Calculator is the time-first sibling — the pair together cover a night completely.

Eclipses need alignment precision beyond a phase model; supermoons need the Moon's distance, which this cycle doesn't track. The calculator names the phase honestly and leaves those events to ephemeris tools — while noting, correctly, that eclipses only ever occur at its two extreme readings.
